---
title: "Paired dot plots"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8.8, fig.height = 4.4, dpi = 100,
  fig.retina = 2, dev = "ragg_png", out.width = "100%"
)
options(gglaplot2.font = "inter")
library(ggplot2)
library(gglaplot2)
```

A paired dot plot shows a measure at two dates for each of a set of
categories: a marker for each date and an arrow from the first to the
second. It reads as "where each borough started and where it got to", which
a grouped bar chart buries and a slope chart cannot carry past a dozen
categories. The web charts draw it horizontally, categories down the side,
ordered by the later value.

## The chart

The data is long, one row per category and date. `geom_gla_paired()` draws
both layers: the arrows in `data-context`, stopping short of the markers,
and the markers coloured by date with the surface as their fill.

```{r paired, fig.height = 3.2}
d <- gla_yearly[gla_yearly$year %in% c(2015, 2024), ]
d$year <- factor(d$year)

ggplot(d, aes(average, series, colour = year)) +
  geom_gla_paired() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = gla_breaks(), labels = label_gla_pounds(short = TRUE)) +
  scale_colour_gla() +
  gla_labs(title = "Every variable fell between 2015 and 2024",
           subtitle = "Yearly average, GBP", source = "LDN Viz Tools demo data",
           x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_gla(gridlines = "x")
```

## Ordering

The web chart orders the categories by their second value, largest at the
top. ggplot2 draws a factor's levels from the bottom up, so compute the
order from the later date and set the levels with it.

```{r ordered, fig.height = 5.5}
set.seed(2)
areas <- c("Barnet", "Camden", "Ealing", "Hackney", "Lambeth", "Newham",
           "Southwark", "Wandsworth")
share <- data.frame(
  area = rep(areas, 2),
  period = rep(c("2019", "2026"), each = length(areas)),
  value = c(runif(8, 0.2, 0.5), runif(8, 0.25, 0.6))
)
later <- share[share$period == "2026", ]
share$area <- factor(share$area, levels = later$area[order(later$value)])

ggplot(share, aes(value, area, colour = period)) +
  geom_gla_paired() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = gla_breaks(), labels = label_gla_percent()) +
  scale_colour_gla() +
  gla_labs(title = "Most areas rose", subtitle = "Share of something, 2019 and 2026",
           source = "Synthetic data", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_gla(gridlines = "x")
```

## A change that crosses zero

When the measure is a change, add the zero rule across the x axis. A
category with a value at only one of the dates keeps its marker and loses
its arrow, so a gap in the data is visible rather than drawn over.

```{r zero, fig.height = 3.2}
change <- d
change$average <- change$average - 30000
change$average[change$series == "Variable C" & change$year == "2015"] <- NA

ggplot(change, aes(average, series, colour = year)) +
  geom_gla_paired() +
  gla_zero_line("x") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = gla_breaks(), labels = label_gla_pounds(short = TRUE)) +
  scale_colour_gla() +
  gla_labs(title = "Against a 30k benchmark", subtitle = "Yearly average less 30,000, GBP",
           note = "Variable C has no 2015 value", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_gla(gridlines = "x")
```

`arrow = FALSE` joins the markers with a plain line, and `inset` sets how far
the connector stops short of them, in pixels.
